questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14056707/assets/0d91ac9127718b0f2755ec14c268d23af810c2ec6f13b4935930b4b348b76b34.png)

The region $D$ in the plane is enclosed between two circles centered at $O$ of radii $1$ and $3,$ as shown above. What is
${∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

The region $D$ represents a portion of the washer enclosed between the circles of radii $1$ and $3$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{ }dA & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ in the third quadrant is enclosed between two quarter-circles centered at $O$ of radii $3$ and $5,$ as shown above. What is 
${∬}_{D}3x\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

The region $D$ represents a portion of the washer enclosed between the circles of radii $3$ and $5$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,3\le r\le 5,\,\pi \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3x\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}3(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{3}^{5}3{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ in the second quadrant is enclosed between two quarter-circles centered at $O$ of radii $3$ and $4,$ as shown above. What is 
${∬}_{D}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

The region $D$ represents a portion of the washer enclosed between the circles of radii $3$ and $4$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,3\le r\le 4,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{3}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Converting an Integral Over a Region Enclosed Between Two Curves to Polar Coordinates
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14056707/assets/51439321ae9d3760eb48d54351dbd519efe290c77d9197ca55aa590ce79e91a8.png)

The region $D$ is enclosed between the curve $(x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ and the line $x=3,$ as shown above. What is
${∬}_{D}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
questions.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(2,0).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For $(x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2)^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =4 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =4 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

- For $x=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3 \\ r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =3 \\ r & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\ r & =3\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(3,-\sqrt{3}).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{6}$ and $\theta =0,$ as depicted below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14056707/assets/bf2d20acbb93d3c61e9890a49d1c15a08c2b4e18b474da421bded7cf3dafc297.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,3\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \le r\le 4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le 0}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{0}{\int }_{3\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\frac{{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{0}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta {\int }_{3\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ is enclosed between the curve ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16$ and the line $x=2\sqrt{2},$ as shown above. What is
${∬}_{D}\frac{y}{x}\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
questions.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $4$ centered at $(0,0).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16,$ we obtain $r=4.$

- For $x=2\sqrt{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\sqrt{2} \\ r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =2\sqrt{2} \\ r & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\ r & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(2\sqrt{2},2\sqrt{2}).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =0$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4},$ as depicted below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14056707/assets/375e270ce444d9f62b50f9a25abfae781113fdad895833d693061ffffe93f5d3.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{y}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{4}r\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta {\int }_{2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{4}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ is enclosed between the curve ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the line $x=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},$ as shown above. What is
${∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
questions.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at $(0,0).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ we obtain $r=1.$

- For $x=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ r & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\ r & =-\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{4}$ and $\theta =\pi ,$ as depicted below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14056707/assets/ca09f228fc218ef1b57196c6b6b1e740c10173b7cd38b1c27407726eccd783f1.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,-\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }{\sqrt{2}}\le r\le 1,\,\frac{3\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /4}^{\pi }{\int }_{-\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta /\sqrt{2}}^{1}\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /4}^{\pi }{\int }_{-\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta /\sqrt{2}}^{1}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ is enclosed between the curve ${x}^{2}+(y+2)^{2}=4$ and the line $y=-3,$ as shown above. What is
${∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
questions.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(0,-2).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+(y+2)^{2}=4,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y+2)^{2} & =4 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2)^{2} & =4 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4 & =4 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}+4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

- For $y=-3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-3 \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-3 \\ r & =-\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ r & =-3\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the points $(-\sqrt{3},-3)$ and $(\sqrt{3},-3).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =-\frac{2\pi }{3}$ and $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{3},$ as depicted below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14056707/assets/5991463a56d8358164d32b15f73e938573463d8d706d2b9c8fc06803326a5f0f.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,-3\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \le r\le -4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,-2\frac{\pi }{3}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{3}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-2\pi /3}^{-\pi /3}{\int }_{-3\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-2\pi /3}^{-\pi /3}{\int }_{-3\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14056707/assets/aed70cc2e5495fcfd9f42ff5d79c3371fb17b62e12ab1909c7738071e59f1a23.png)

The region $D$ is enclosed between the curve $(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=2$ and the line $y=x+2,$ as shown above. What is
${∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
questions.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at $(-1,1).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For $(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=2,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =2 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1)^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)^{2} & =2 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2 & =2 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-2r(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-2r(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0 \\ r(r-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ).$

- For $y=x+2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x+2 \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2 \\ r(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =2 \\ r & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the points $(-2,0)$ and $(0,2).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $\theta =\pi ,$ as depicted below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14056707/assets/b9c2cd48302ef8d4e2d5e65a56d19506600c5e6552a4d9a1ef7d578a09a21557.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\le r\le 2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{2/(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{2/(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\frac{4y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at $(0,1).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =1 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)^{2} & =1 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1 & =1 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

- For $y=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =1 \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ r & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ r & =\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(-1,1).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{4},$ as depicted below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14056707/assets/1b83e2674bba4bd6c326083f8c94496b5288de23575dc63a92b9a660eba69f67.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \le r\le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{4}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{4y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}{\int }_{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [r]_{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-2[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )]_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4} \\  & =-2[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )] \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6}{\int }_{-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [r]_{-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (2+\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\theta ]_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6} \\  & =[(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{6})-\frac{\pi }{3})-(0-\pi )] \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}-2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}

The region $D$ in the first quadrant is enclosed between the quarter-circles of radii $3$ and $4,$ as shown above. What is
$\displaystyle \iint\limits_D \dfrac{1}{x^2+y^2} \: \textrm{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

The region $D$ represents a portion of the washer enclosed between the circles of radii $3$ and $4$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \Big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 3 \leq r \leq 4, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2} \Big\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{r}{{r}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{1}{r}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Over a Region Enclosed Between Two Curves
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14056707/assets/aa730804a15decac8450255e714ca1e0697f4f2326eb615d4d035a2870a49dce.png)

Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_D \dfrac{2y}{x^2+y^2} \: \textrm{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\dfrac{1}{2}$ centered at $\left(0,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\!.$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For $x^2+\left( y-\dfrac{1}{2} \right)^2=\dfrac14,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r = \sin\theta.$

- For $y=\dfrac{1}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2} \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{2} \\ r & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ r & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta.$ Our curves intersect at the point $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{1}{2}\right).$ So, the entire region lies between the radial lines $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ as depicted below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14056707/assets/1284a8b4b3f1634b4f7586d40ab8adf9cf93c69484b7ed069f138c8055e88892.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$ as 

$$
\Delta = \Big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: \dfrac{1}{2}\csc\theta \leq r \leq \sin\theta, \: \dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2} \Big\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1/2\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{1/2\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [r]_{1/2\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )]_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(0-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
